about: Lesson X3 (x03-transitions-history), side-topic shelf, Foundations, D1. Adoption curves of the United States as shares over time, each point transcribed from a dated primary source (the Census Bureau's Historical Statistics and decennial housing tables, EIA's Electric Power Annual); solar's share is our arithmetic on EIA's table. Diffusion only: no cost curve of any technology and no forecast of future speed.

series.label: Homes with electric service
series.measure: the share of all homes (dwelling units) with electric service

series.label: Town and other non-farm homes with electric service
series.measure: the share of town and other non-farm homes (urban and rural non-farm dwelling units) with electric service

series.label: Farm homes with electric service
series.measure: the share of farm homes (farm dwelling units) with electric service

series.label: Homes heated mainly with piped gas
series.measure: the share of occupied homes heated mainly with piped gas (the census's utility gas); the 1940 figure also counts bottled gas, so 1940 is not like for like

series.label: Homes heated mainly with coal or coke
series.measure: the share of occupied homes heated mainly with coal or coke (a fuel made by baking coal)

series.label: Families owning a car
series.measure: the share of families owning at least one car, from a household survey that began in 1947; Alaska and Hawaii are left out

series.label: Solar's share of U.S. electricity
series.measure: solar generation from utility-scale plants (1 MW or larger) and from small systems, including rooftop panels, as a share of all U.S. generation (our arithmetic on EIA's table)

solarRaw.rule: share = estimated total solar ÷ (utility-scale total generation + estimated small-scale solar PV)

heatOthers.note: the other main heating fuels in the national rows, %, to say which fuel was most common

cards.text: Wires had to reach every farm, spread across the countryside
cards.why: Farms passed half about 25 years after town homes did (Series S 110 and S 111).

cards.text: Public loans for rural power lines under the Rural Electrification Act of 1936
cards.why: EIA credits rural electrification: almost half of farms had power by 1942, against 11% in 1932.

cards.text: Gas pipelines built across the country in the 1950s and 1960s
cards.why: EIA reported in March 2024 that about half of the long-distance gas pipeline network went in then; gas overtook coal for heating between the 1950 and 1960 censuses.

cards.text: A cheaper or better service people wanted, such as better light or heat
cards.why: Fouquet (2010, abstract), on British transitions from 1500 to 1920: the main economic drivers were opportunities to produce cheaper or better energy services.

cards.text: A new source had to be refined, gradually, until it could compete
cards.why: Fouquet (2010, abstract), on British transitions from 1500 to 1920: small early markets willing to pay more let new sources be refined gradually; on average the whole innovation chain took over 100 years.

timeline.label: Coal at 9% of U.S. energy
timeline.text: Coal supplied 9% of U.S. energy use, and 27% by 1870 as railroads spread.

timeline.label: Pearl Street Station
timeline.text: One of the world's first central power plants opened in New York; it could power 5,000 lights.

timeline.label: Coal passes wood
timeline.text: Around 1885 coal passed wood as the largest U.S. energy source.

timeline.label: 8% of homes have electric service
timeline.text: The first year of the Census Bureau's series of homes with electric service.

timeline.label: Model T
timeline.text: Ford first produced the Model T car.

timeline.label: Rural Electrification Act
timeline.text: A law aimed at bringing electricity to farms across the country.

timeline.label: Petroleum passes coal
timeline.text: Petroleum became the most-used U.S. energy source, and has been ever since.

timeline.label: Interstate Highway System
timeline.text: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 established the Interstate Highway System.

timeline.label: Natural gas passes coal
timeline.text: Natural gas passed coal in U.S. energy use; it has been second most years since.

timeline.label: Gas heats most homes
timeline.text: Piped gas heated 55.2% of homes and coal or coke 2.9%, against 11.3% (with bottled gas) and 54.7% in 1940.

timeline.label: Renewables pass coal
timeline.text: U.S. energy use from renewables passed coal for the first time since the 1880s.

timeline.label: Solar at 8.7% of electricity
timeline.text: Solar made 8.7% of U.S. electricity, large plants and small systems together (our arithmetic).

debate.title: How fast were past transitions? Two readings of the same record

sides.title: Sovacool (2016)
points: The usual view: energy transitions are slow, often taking decades to centuries.
Some newer evidence does not fit that view, so a transition needs a clear definition before its speed is judged.

sides.title: Grubler, Wilson and Nemet (2016)
points: Slow and fast examples are often measured, defined and explained in different ways.
Setting them side by side then compares unlike things: apples and oranges.

debate.note: Both from each paper's summary; the lesson takes no side. Homes with electric service and solar's share of electricity measure different things, so their slopes alone cannot say which spread faster.

stop.title: This side topic stops at reading the curves
stop.lede: Adoption enters the course only as diffusion, a share over time; costs and forecasts stay out.
includes: What share of homes, families or electricity each change reached, and when.
What sped some curves up and held others back, read from dated sources.
Why the answer to 'how fast' depends on what you measure.
leaves: How the cost of any technology changed over time.
Forecasts of how fast anything spreads next.
Economic history beyond these curves: prices, wages, trade.

facts.what: From 8% of U.S. homes with electric service in 1907 to 90%, passed between 1945 (85.0%) and 1950 (94.0%).
How far farms trailed town homes: town and other non-farm homes passed half between 1920 and 1925, farm homes between 1945 and 1950.
Homes heated mainly with coal or coke, 1940 to 1970, while piped gas rose from 11.3% (1940, with bottled gas) to 55.2%.
Coal passed wood as the largest U.S. energy source around 1885; petroleum passed coal in 1950.
Solar's share of U.S. electricity in 2025, large plants and small systems such as rooftop panels together (our arithmetic on EIA's table).
